name: Sonnet global diversification via US-listed ADRs and ETFs
strategy: A quality-tilted basket of individual US-listed ADRs spanning Europe and developed Asia (semis, enterprise software, pharma, staples, electronics), sized conservatively with a large cash buffer against a still-hawkish Fed and firm dollar.
reassessment_note: The book I inherited (XLF/XBI long, SOXL/GDX short) is a pure US domestic-sector relative-value trade -- it has nothing to do with the mandate this packet is named for (global diversification via US-listed ADRs and ETFs) and has also lost money (-2.51% NAV) doing something outside that mandate. I am replacing it wholesale with a basket that is actually what the name says: individual quality non-US ADRs, chosen to diversify by company and geography rather than duplicate my Round 2 book's country-ETF approach (EEM/TSM/EWZ/EWJ/INDA/SQQQ). There is zero symbol overlap between the two books, so the >=50% same-direction gross-weight divergence required by the Round 3 novelty rule is trivially satisfied while both books still share one macro read: the 2026-09-16 FOMC stayed hawkish, 2yr yields are at their highest since mid-2024, the 10yr is near 5%, and the dollar index is firm near 99.9 with the BOJ's hawkish dissent adding yen volatility -- so this book leans on names whose theses are company-specific and less purely dollar/EM-beta (ASML's AI/lithography capex cycle, SAP's cloud transition, a contrarian NVO turnaround, UL as defensive ballast, SONY for AI image-sensor demand) and keeps 42% in cash rather than replicating a second EM-beta book. Position sizing is meaningfully smaller and gross exposure (58%) meaningfully lower than the book I am replacing (85% gross), reflecting that a hawkish Fed with a still-firm dollar is not an environment to lean hard into directional shorts on volatile leveraged/commodity vehicles (SOXL, GDX) that were outside the mandate to begin with.

positions.thesis: ASML is the sole supplier of EUV lithography tools and is mid-cycle on a multi-year AI/leading-edge semiconductor capex supercycle: it and TSMC just announced a joint roadmap to move High-NA EUV from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks by 2031, and Samsung is expanding its High-NA commitment for 2028 DRAM production, both signaling multi-year forward demand visibility rather than a near-term cyclical peak. Shares trade near $1,679 with an active, ongoing buyback program (repurchases through September at ~EUR1,464-1,512), evidence management sees value even at current levels. This is the highest-conviction, largest-weighted leg because its secular driver (AI/leading-edge fab capex) is largely independent of Fed rate policy, unlike EM-beta names. Stop at -12% and take-profit at +30% given the stock's elevated absolute price and volatility around any global semi-capex sentiment wobble.

SAP is Europe's dominant enterprise software franchise, mid-transition from on-prem ERP to cloud/AI-embedded subscription revenue, which gives it a domestically-anchored (euro-area corporate IT spend) earnings stream that is less correlated to the dollar-strength/EM-stress dynamic currently pressuring Indian and broader EM assets. It diversifies this book's factor exposure away from both US mega-cap tech concentration and pure EM beta, which is the point of a global-ADR mandate. Sized below ASML given less explicit near-term catalyst flow; stop -10%/TP +20% is a standard quality-compounder band.

Novo Nordisk is a contrarian value entry: shares sit near $43, a fraction of prior highs after 2025's GLP-1 competitive setbacks versus Eli Lilly, but the news flow has turned constructive in the last two weeks -- CHMP recommended EU approval for Sogroya in pediatric short stature, FREHEMGO (denecimig) got a positive CHMP opinion with an expected Q4 2026 EU launch, and Phase 3 STEP Young data showed 40.4% of adolescents on semaglutide were no longer classified as obese versus 0% on placebo. A beaten-down pharma leader with a reloading regulatory pipeline is a legitimate global-diversification building block distinct from anything in the Round 2 book. Wider stop (-15%) reflects the stock's still-elevated volatility post-selloff; TP +35% reflects real turnaround upside if sentiment normalizes.

Unilever is UK/Netherlands-domiciled global consumer staples -- low-beta, demand-inelastic revenue that historically holds up better than cyclicals or EM equities when the Fed stays hawkish and global growth data wobbles. It is the defensive ballast leg of this book, intentionally low-volatility (tight 8% stop, modest 15% take-profit) to offset the higher-beta ASML/NVO/SONY legs and to diversify the mandate's ADR sleeve into a sector this manager's Round 2 book does not touch at all.

Sony gives Japan/developed-Asia exposure that is deliberately not EWJ (already the vehicle in the Round 2 book): it is a company-specific bet on Sony's dominant position in CMOS image sensors, where demand is accelerating from AI-enabled smartphones, robotics, and automotive/data-center vision applications, alongside a resilient gaming and music/entertainment franchise. The real risk flagged by this week's research is BOJ policy: a hawkish BOJ dissent this week pushed the dollar higher against the yen, and further yen strength from BOJ tightening could pressure Sony's USD-translated earnings, or yen weakness could pressure the ADR's local-currency read-through -- either way this is a two-sided FX risk that is why the stop is kept relatively tight at -12% against a smaller 8% position size.
